entries.capture: name '(?<name>[^']+)' is not defined(?:\. Did you mean: '(?<suggestion>[^']+)'\?)?
entries.title: NameError: name is not defined
entries.explain: Python looked for this name in the current function, then the module, then the built-ins, and found nothing. Names exist only after the line that assigns or imports them has run.
causes: A typo or different capitalization (`Total` vs `total`, `true` vs `True`).
Using a variable before the line that assigns it, or using a local variable from another function.
Forgetting an `import` (`math.sqrt` without `import math`).
Text without quotes, so Python reads it as a name: `print(hello)`.
fix: Check the spelling against where the name is created; Python often suggests a close match.
Assign or import it before the line that uses it.
Put text in quotes: `print("hello")`.
entries.before:
def area(r):
    return pi * r ** 2   # NameError: pi
entries.specific: `{name}` does not exist at the point it is used{onLine}.

entries.title: UnboundLocalError: local variable referenced before assignment
entries.explain: If a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, Python treats that name as local to the whole function. So reading it before that assignment fails, even though a global with the same name exists.
causes: `count += 1` inside a function, where `count` is a module-level variable.
Assigning the variable only inside an `if` branch that did not run.
A loop that runs zero times, so its variable is never set.
fix: Pass the value in and return the new one: `def add(count): return count + 1`.
If you really mean the module variable, declare `global count` (or `nonlocal` in a nested function).
Give the variable a value before any branch.
entries.after:
count = 0
def click(count):
    return count + 1
count = click(count)
entries.specific: `{name}` is local to the function (it is assigned there) but read before it gets a value{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: unsupported operand type(s)
entries.explain: The operator is not defined for this pair of types. Python never converts between text and numbers automatically, so `"3" + 1` or `5 - "2"` fail.
causes: Mixing numbers with strings from `input()`, which always returns `str`.
One side is `None` because a function had no `return`.
Adding a list and a number, or subtracting strings.
fix: Convert explicitly: `int(text)`, `float(text)` or `str(number)`.
If one side is `NoneType`, find the function that should have returned a value.
entries.before:
age = input("Age: ")
next_year = age + 1   # str + int
entries.specific: `{op}` cannot combine a `{left}` and a `{right}`{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
entries.explain: `+` between two strings joins them, but Python will not silently turn a number (or anything else) into text to join it. Both sides must be the same kind of sequence.
causes: Building a message with `+` and a number: `"Total: " + total`.
Adding a single item to a list with `+` instead of `append`.
fix: Use an f-string: `f"Total: {total}"`.
Or convert: `"Total: " + str(total)`.
For lists: `items.append(x)` or `items + [x]`.
entries.specific: A `{other}` is joined to a `{kind}` with `+`{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable
entries.explain: The code used `[ ]` on a value that is `None`. Usually a function that was expected to return a list or dict returned nothing, or an in-place method's result was stored.
causes: A function that has no `return` (or a path without one) returns `None`.
Storing the result of an in-place method: `items = items.sort()` makes `items` `None`.
A lookup such as `d.get(key)` or `re.match(...)` that found nothing.
fix: Make the function return its value on every path.
Call in-place methods on their own line (`items.sort()`), or use `sorted(items)`.
Check for `None` before indexing: `if match is not None:`.
entries.before:
scores = [3, 1, 2]
scores = scores.sort()
print(scores[0])   # scores is None
entries.specific: The value indexed with `[ ]`{onLine} is `None`.

entries.title: TypeError: object is not subscriptable
entries.explain: Only containers such as lists, tuples, strings and dicts support `[ ]`. This value's type does not, so there is nothing to index.
causes: Indexing a number: `n[0]` on an `int`.
Indexing a function or method instead of calling it: `get_items[0]` instead of `get_items()[0]`.
Indexing a `set`, which has no order.
fix: Convert numbers to text first: `str(n)[0]`.
Call functions with `()` before indexing.
Turn a set into a list (`sorted(s)[0]`) if you need positions.
entries.specific: A `{type}` is indexed with `[ ]`{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: missing required positional argument
entries.explain: The function declares parameters without default values, and the call did not pass a value for some of them.
causes: Calling with too few arguments.
Calling a method on the class instead of an instance (`Dog.bark()`), so `self` takes the place of the first argument.
Forgetting to pass arguments when creating an object, so `__init__` is missing them.
fix: Pass every required argument, or give the parameter a default: `def greet(name="friend"):`.
Create an instance first and call methods on it: `Dog().bark()`.
entries.specific: `{func}()` was called without {names}{onLine}.

entries.message: (?<func>[\w.<>]+)\(\) takes (?<takes>\d+|from \d+ to \d+) positional arguments? but (?<given>\d+) (?:were|was) given
entries.title: TypeError: takes N positional arguments but M were given
entries.explain: The call passes more positional arguments than the function accepts. With methods, remember that Python passes the instance as the first argument (`self`) automatically, so it counts too.
causes: A method defined without `self`: `def bark():` inside a class.
Passing an extra argument, or arguments meant for a different function.
Passing a list's items separately where the function takes one list.
fix: Add `self` as the first parameter of every method.
Match the call to the function's parameters.
entries.specific: `{func}()` takes {takes} positional arguments but got {given}{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: object is not iterable
entries.explain: A `for` loop, unpacking, `list()`, `sum()` or `in` needs something it can step through item by item. This value is a single thing, such as a number or `None`.
causes: Looping over a number: `for i in 5:` instead of `for i in range(5):`.
Looping over `None` returned by a function without `return`.
Unpacking a single value: `a, b = 7`.
fix: Use `range(n)` to loop a number of times.
Make sure the function returns the list or other collection.
entries.specific: A `{type}` is used{onLine} where something to loop over is needed.

entries.title: TypeError: object is not callable
entries.explain: Parentheses after a value call it like a function. This value is not a function, often because a variable has the same name as a function and replaced it.
causes: Shadowing a built-in: `list = [1, 2]` and later `list(...)`; or `sum = 0` and later `sum(...)`.
Calling a value by mistake: `total(5)` where `total` is a number, or `5(2 + 3)` for multiplication.
Calling a property or attribute: `obj.name()` where `name` is a string.
fix: Rename the variable so it does not reuse a function's name (`numbers`, `total`).
Use `*` for multiplication: `5 * (2 + 3)`.
Drop the `()` when reading an attribute.
entries.before:
sum = 0
print(sum([1, 2, 3]))   # sum is now an int
entries.specific: A `{type}` is called like a function{onLine}.

entries.title: TypeError: wrong type for this operation
entries.explain: An operation or function received a value of a type it cannot work with. Python checks types when the line runs, and the message says which types met.
causes: Mixing text and numbers without converting.
Passing the wrong kind of argument to a function, or `None` where a value was expected.
Calling something that is not a function, or indexing something that is not a container.
fix: Read the message: it names the operation and the types involved.
Print `type(x)` for the values on that line to see what they really are.
entries.specific: Python says: {detail}.

entries.title: AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute
entries.explain: The code used `.something` on a value that is `None`. Something that should have produced an object produced nothing instead.
causes: Storing the result of an in-place method: `items = items.append(x)` sets `items` to `None`.
A function without `return` on some path.
`re.match(...)` or `dict.get(...)` found nothing and returned `None`.
fix: Call in-place methods (`append`, `sort`, `reverse`, `update`) without assigning their result.
Return a value on every path.
Check for `None` first: `if m is not None:`.
entries.before:
items = []
items = items.append(1)
items.append(2)   # items is None
entries.specific: `.{attr}` is used on a value that is `None`{onLine}.

entries.capture: '(?<type>[^']+)' object has no attribute '(?<attr>[^']+)'|module '(?<module>[^']+)' has no attribute '(?<mattr>[^']+)'
entries.title: AttributeError: object has no attribute
entries.explain: The value has no attribute or method with this name. Each type has its own set of methods, and names from other languages often do not exist in Python.
causes: A method from another language: `list.push` (Python uses `append`), `str.length` (use `len(s)`).
A typo, or an attribute set in `__init__` under a different name.
The value is a different type than you think (a `str` instead of a `list`).
Your file has the same name as a module (`random.py`), so `import random` imports your file.
fix: Check the spelling, and use `dir(value)` to list what it has.
Use Python's names: `append`, `len()`, `upper()`.
Rename files that shadow standard modules.
entries.specific: A `{type}` has no attribute `{attr}`{onLine}.

entries.title: KeyError: key not found in dictionary
entries.explain: Reading `d[key]` requires the key to be in the dictionary. It is not, so Python raises `KeyError` with the missing key as its message.
causes: The key was never added, or differs in spelling, case or type (`"1"` vs `1`).
Extra whitespace in a key read from a file or input.
Reading before the code that fills the dictionary has run.
fix: Use `d.get(key, default)` when a missing key is normal.
Check with `if key in d:` first.
For counting, use `d[key] = d.get(key, 0) + 1`, or `collections.Counter` / `defaultdict`.
entries.specific: The dictionary has no key `{key}`{onLine}.

entries.capture: (?<kind>list|string|tuple|range object|deque) index out of range|(?<pop>pop from empty list)
entries.title: IndexError: index out of range
entries.explain: Positions in a list, tuple or string run from `0` to `len(x) - 1`. The code used a position at or past `len(x)` (or below `-len(x)`), so there is no item there.
causes: Using `len(items)` as an index; the last item is `items[len(items) - 1]`, or simply `items[-1]`.
A `range` that goes one step too far.
The list is empty, so even `items[0]` fails.
Removing items from a list while looping over its indexes.
fix: Loop over items directly: `for item in items:`, or `for i, item in enumerate(items):`.
Use `items[-1]` for the last item, after checking `if items:`.
entries.specific: A {kind} was read past its end{onLine}.

entries.message: (?:invalid literal for int\(\) with base \d+|could not convert string to float): (?<value>.+)
entries.title: ValueError: invalid literal for int()
entries.explain: `int()` and `float()` accept only text that looks exactly like a number. The text contains something else, such as letters, a unit, a comma, or a decimal point for `int()`, or it is empty.
causes: Input with extra characters: `"12a"`, `"5 kg"`, `"1,000"`.
An empty string, for example from pressing Enter or a blank line in a file.
`int("3.5")`: `int` does not accept a decimal point (use `float` first, or `int(float(s))`).
fix: Clean the text first (`s.strip()`, remove units or commas).
Wrap the conversion in `try` / `except ValueError` to handle bad input.
Use `float()` for decimal numbers.
entries.specific: The text {value} is not a valid number{onLine}.

entries.message: too many values to unpack \(expected (?<expected>\d+)(?:, got (?<got>\d+))?\)
entries.title: ValueError: too many values to unpack
entries.explain: Unpacking (`a, b = something`) needs exactly as many names on the left as items on the right. The right side has more items than there are names.
causes: `a, b = line.split(",")` where the line has more than one comma.
Looping over a dict with `for k, v in d:` (that gives keys only; use `d.items()`).
A function that returns more values than you unpack.
fix: Match the number of names, or collect the rest: `first, *rest = values`.
Use `d.items()` to get key/value pairs.
For split, limit it: `line.split(",", 1)`.
entries.specific: The unpacking{onLine} has {expected} names but more values.

entries.message: not enough values to unpack \(expected (?<expected>\d+), got (?<got>\d+)\)
entries.title: ValueError: not enough values to unpack
entries.explain: Unpacking (`a, b, c = something`) needs exactly as many items on the right as names on the left. The right side has fewer items.
causes: `name, age = line.split(",")` on a line without a comma (often an empty or header line).
A function that returns fewer values than you unpack.
Data rows of uneven length.
fix: Check the length first, or skip blank lines: `if not line.strip(): continue`.
Unpack with a star to tolerate fewer items: `name, *rest = parts`.
For one separator, `str.partition` always returns three parts: `name, _, age = line.partition(",")`.
entries.after:
line = "Ann"
name, _, age = line.partition(",")   # age is ""
entries.specific: The unpacking{onLine} expected {expected} values but got {got}.

entries.title: ValueError: right type, wrong value
entries.explain: A function received a value of the correct type, but the value itself is not acceptable, such as `list.remove(x)` for an item not in the list, or `math.sqrt(-1)`.
causes: `items.remove(x)` or `items.index(x)` where `x` is not in the list.
A math function outside its domain (`math.sqrt(-1)`, `math.log(0)`).
Parsing text that is in the wrong format (dates, numbers).
fix: Check before calling: `if x in items: items.remove(x)`.
Or catch `ValueError` where bad input is expected.
entries.specific: Python says: {detail}.

entries.title: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
entries.explain: `/`, `//` and `%` cannot divide by zero; there is no answer, so Python raises an error. This applies to floats too: `1.0 / 0` also raises.
causes: Averaging an empty list: `sum(xs) / len(xs)` with `len(xs) == 0`.
A divisor that comes from input or a calculation and happens to be `0`.
fix: Check the divisor first: `avg = sum(xs) / len(xs) if xs else 0`.
Or catch `ZeroDivisionError` where zero is a valid input.
entries.after:
scores = []
average = sum(scores) / len(scores) if scores else 0
entries.specific: A division{onLine} had zero on the right.

entries.title: IndentationError: unexpected indent
entries.explain: In Python, indentation is part of the syntax: it shows which lines belong to a block. This line is indented more than the line before it, but nothing (such as an `if` or `def` ending in `:`) opened a new block.
causes: A stray space or tab at the start of a line.
Pasted code with different indentation.
A line that was part of a block whose header line was deleted.
fix: Line the statement up with its neighbours at the same level.
Use 4 spaces per level consistently.
entries.specific: Line {line} is indented, but no block was opened above it.

entries.message: expected an indented block(?: after '?(?<what>[^']+?)'? (?:statement |definition )?on line (?<header>\d+))?
entries.title: IndentationError: expected an indented block
entries.explain: A line ending in `:` (`if`, `for`, `def`, `class`, `while`, `try`) must be followed by at least one indented line, its body. The next line is not indented.
causes: Forgetting to indent the body.
An empty function or branch you meant to fill in later.
Commented-out body lines, which do not count.
fix: Indent the body by 4 spaces.
For an intentionally empty block, write `pass`.
entries.specific: The `{what}` block that starts on line {header} has no indented body.

entries.title: IndentationError: indentation does not line up
entries.explain: Python uses indentation to group lines into blocks, and each line must line up exactly with a level used above it. Most often this is "unindent does not match any outer indentation level": a line is dedented to a column no earlier block used.
causes: Mixing 2 and 4 spaces, or spaces and tabs, in the same block.
A line dedented part of the way, between two levels.
fix: Re-indent the block with 4 spaces per level; most editors can convert tabs to spaces for the whole file.
entries.specific: Line {line} does not line up with any indentation level above it.

entries.title: TabError: inconsistent use of tabs and spaces
entries.explain: Python cannot tell how deep a line is when one block mixes tabs and spaces, because a tab has no fixed width. It refuses to guess.
causes: Code pasted from another source that used tabs.
An editor that inserts tabs on some lines and spaces on others.
fix: Convert all indentation to spaces (4 per level); editors have a "Convert indentation to spaces" command.
Turn on visible whitespace to spot the tabs.
entries.specific: Line {line} mixes tabs and spaces with the lines around it.

entries.title: SyntaxError: bracket was never closed
entries.explain: An opening bracket was never matched by its closing partner, so Python reached the end of the file (or a line it cannot fit) still inside the bracket.
causes: A missing `)` at the end of a call, often with nested calls: `print(len(items)`.
A list or dict literal missing its `]` or `}`.
fix: Add the closing bracket; count opening and closing brackets on the line Python points to.
entries.specific: The `{bracket}`{onLine} has no matching closing bracket.

entries.title: SyntaxError: unterminated string literal
entries.explain: A string started with a quote but the line ended before a matching closing quote. Ordinary strings must close on the same line they open.
causes: A missing closing quote.
Mismatched quotes: `'hello"`.
An apostrophe inside a single-quoted string: `'it's'`.
A backslash before the closing quote (`"C:\"`), which escapes it.
fix: Close the string with the same quote you opened it with.
Use the other quote type when the text contains one: `"it's"`.
Use triple quotes for text spanning lines.
entries.specific: A string starting{onLine} is never closed.

entries.title: SyntaxError: expected ':'
entries.explain: Lines that open a block (`if`, `elif`, `else`, `for`, `while`, `def`, `class`, `try`, `except`, `with`) must end with a colon. This one does not.
causes: A forgotten `:` at the end of the line.
Something else on the line confused Python, such as `=` instead of `==` in an `if`.
fix: Add `:` at the end of the block's first line.
entries.specific: Line {line} needs a `:` at its end.

entries.title: SyntaxError: invalid syntax
entries.explain: Python could not read the line as code at all, so nothing ran. The `^` marker in the message shows where Python gave up; the real mistake is often just before it, or at the end of the previous line.
causes: A missing comma, operator, bracket or quote.
`=` used inside a condition where `==` was meant.
A keyword used as a name (`class = 3`) or a keyword from another language (`else if` instead of `elif`).
An unclosed bracket on the previous line.
fix: Look at the spot the `^` marks, then at the line above it.
Use `elif`, `==` for comparisons, and commas between list items.
entries.specific: Python could not read line {line}; check that line and the end of the one before it.

entries.title: SyntaxError: the code could not be parsed
entries.explain: Python reads the whole file before running anything, and this line is not valid Python. Nothing in the file ran.
causes: A missing or extra bracket, quote, colon or comma.
A keyword in the wrong place, or a statement that belongs to another language.
fix: Read the message and look where the `^` points, then at the line before.
entries.specific: Python says: {detail}.

entries.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named
entries.explain: Python searched its import path and found no module or package with this name. Either the name is misspelled, the package is not installed for the Python that runs your code, or a local file is not where Python looks.
causes: A typo or wrong name: the install name can differ from the import name (`pip install beautifulsoup4`, `import bs4`).
A third-party package that is not installed in the environment running the code.
Your own module in another folder, outside the import path.
fix: Check the spelling and the module's real import name.
Install it for the same interpreter: `python -m pip install <package>`.
Prefer the standard library when it covers what you need (`json`, `csv`, `math`, `collections`).
entries.specific: No module called `{module}` can be found.

entries.title: ImportError: cannot import name
entries.explain: The module was found, but it has no attribute with the name you asked for in `from module import name`.
causes: A typo or wrong casing in the imported name.
The name lives in a different module (`from math import randint`; it is in `random`).
Two of your modules import each other (a circular import), so one is only half-loaded.
Your own file shadows the real module (`random.py` in your folder).
fix: Check the spelling and which module defines the name.
Break circular imports by moving shared code into a third module, or import inside the function that needs it.
Rename files that clash with standard modules.
entries.specific: `{module}` has no `{name}` to import.

entries.title: RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
entries.explain: A function kept calling itself and went past Python's limit (about 1000 nested calls by default). Almost always the recursion has no stopping case, or never reaches it.
causes: No base case: the function always calls itself.
The base case is never reached, for example `n - 1` on a negative `n`, or the argument does not change.
A property or `__getattr__` that refers to itself.
fix: Add a base case that returns without recursing, and make each call move toward it.
For very deep work, use a loop instead of recursion.
entries.specific: The recursion{onLine} never stops.

entries.title: FileNotFoundError: No such file or directory
entries.explain: `open()` (in read mode) or another file function was given a path that does not exist. A relative path is resolved from the current working directory, which is not necessarily the folder your script is in.
causes: A typo in the file name or extension.
A relative path resolved from a different working directory.
Writing into a folder that does not exist (`open("out/a.txt", "w")` without `out/`).
fix: Print `os.getcwd()` or `Path("data.txt").resolve()` to see where Python is looking.
Build the path from the script's folder: `Path(__file__).parent / "data.txt"`.
Create folders first: `Path("out").mkdir(exist_ok=True)`.
entries.after:
from pathlib import Path
Path("out").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
with open("out/report.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("done")
entries.specific: Nothing exists at `{path}`.

entries.title: StopIteration: the iterator is exhausted
entries.explain: `next()` asks an iterator for its next item. There are none left (or there never were), so the iterator signals the end by raising `StopIteration`. `for` loops handle this for you; calling `next()` yourself does not.
causes: `next(iter(items))` on an empty collection.
`next(x for x in items if ...)` when nothing matches.
Reusing an iterator or generator that a previous loop already consumed.
fix: Give `next` a default: `next((x for x in items if x > 10), None)`.
Recreate the generator if you need to loop again, or store results in a list.
entries.before:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
big = next(n for n in nums if n > 10)
entries.after:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
big = next((n for n in nums if n > 10), None)
entries.specific: `next()` was called{onLine} on an iterator with no items left.

entries.title: JSONDecodeError: invalid JSON
entries.explain: `json.loads()` or `json.load()` was given text that is not valid JSON. JSON is stricter than Python syntax: double quotes only, no trailing commas, `true`/`false`/`null` in lower case.
causes: Empty text, which gives "Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0)".
Single quotes or a Python dict printed with `str()` (`{'a': 1}`, `True`, `None`).
A trailing comma, or HTML (such as an error page) instead of JSON.
fix: Print the text before parsing to see what it really is.
Produce JSON with `json.dumps()`, not `str()`.
Catch `json.JSONDecodeError` for input you do not control.
entries.specific: Parsing failed at line {jline}, column {jcol} of the JSON text: {problem}.

entries.title: AssertionError: an assert failed
entries.explain: An `assert condition` statement found its condition false. Asserts state something the code assumes is always true, so a failure means either the code or the assumption is wrong.
causes: A value is different from what the assert (or a test) expected.
An earlier step produced bad data that only the assert noticed.
`assert (x, "msg")` with parentheses: that asserts a tuple, which is always true, so it never fires (Python warns).
fix: Print or inspect the values in the condition to see which part is false.
Give asserts a message: `assert total >= 0, f"total was {total}"`.
Do not rely on `assert` for input validation: it is skipped when Python runs with `-O`.
entries.specific: The assertion message says: {detail}.

entries.title: RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration
entries.explain: A loop over a dict or set added or removed entries in that same dict or set. Python cannot keep its place when the collection's size changes under it, so it stops.
causes: `del d[k]` or `d.pop(k)` inside `for k in d:`.
Adding new keys inside the loop.
fix: Loop over a copy of the keys: `for k in list(d):`.
Or build a new dict: `d = {k: v for k, v in d.items() if v > 0}`.
entries.after:
stock = {"apple": 0, "pear": 2}
stock = {k: v for k, v in stock.items() if v != 0}
entries.specific: A {kind} was changed while being looped over{onLine}.
